old-lamp-seller.guess: That wisps are flames that slipped their wicks and went looking for another, since a flame only ever borrows its wick.
invented: She cuts and twists every wick she sells herself, and has trimmed wicks since she was six.
She cut four of the wicks in the captain's ship lamps.
She has sent the lamplighter wicks for the dead post for twenty years and keeps a tally; the one Io carries is the three hundredth.
Her mother told her the second half of a wick always burns quicker.
Tonight she keeps a chalk mark on her counter for every lamp the four bring home.

lines.text: Evening. I've held up a feather, shut my wagon door and stood in front of them. They still lean. Your turn, Jester.
There you are at last. I've cut every wick on this counter short, so there's less flame for anything to get hold of.
You've gone past my stall nine times tonight. On the tenth, I thought, she'll stop. And here you are.
A flame leans for wind, or a door, or somebody breathing on it. I've never seen one lean for nothing. Not in my life.
Two of those cold lights came through at supper. Every flame on my counter shrank to a bead till they'd gone.
The captain's lamps? I cut four of those wicks. A good wick never leaves its lamp. Something took them by the flame.
My guess? Those cold lights are flames that slipped their wicks. A flame only ever borrows a wick, you know.
I've sold nine lamps tonight. Nobody buys a lamp at night. They want something to hold, I think, not to light.
I've a chalk mark on the counter for every lamp you bring home. Don't make me run out of counter.
Twelve home and tied down with blue thread. I'd have built wire cages. Twelve of them. I'd still be at it.
My flames still lean, mind. Less. Like someone told to sit down who keeps looking at the door.
Every flame in the square is lying near flat toward that hill. I've stopped trimming. You can't trim for that.
I've counted every minute since the ship went up. I'll not tell you how many. Sit, before I start again.
Thirty-one flames on my counter, standing straight up. I've never been so glad of a dull flame in my life.
Somebody will have to keep that new flame on the crag. It'll want a decent wick. I've set my best aside.
Twice in one night. Don't cast near my counter, mind. When you do, every flame I've got bows down to the wick.
I've put a wick by for your wagon lamp. Short, tight twist. It's the sort that stays where it's put.
My hands have trimmed wicks since I was six and never once shook. Tonight they shook. Twice. I counted.
You've stood at my stall more tonight than the captain has in all his years, and he buys wicks.
Won, have you? You've come back brighter than you went. I notice a flame grow by a hair, and I noticed.
Knocked flat, and upright again already. I'd sell a wick that did that for double.
One of you is burning low. A quarter of a wick left, I'd say. Rest before you gutter.
Your stool's been empty so long a cat took it. I've moved the cat.
You've been out to the lamplighter. Did she ask after me? No. She'll have asked after the wick.
The fortune-teller's had you in, then. She'll have charged a coin to tell you it's dark out. I'll tell you for nothing.
The right size for once, she says? It's the same size I've sent her for twenty years. The cheek of the woman.
So Io warmed one till it went home? Then they want a wick to come back to. I've a drawerful.
New wicks, you four. Bright, and a bit too eager. That burns down to something steadier.
I used to lose three flames every time you fought in the ring. Now it's one. You've stopped wasting sky.
When you four walk past now my flames stand up straight, like they're being inspected. They never did that for anyone.
Six. Exactly half. My mother always said the second half of a wick burns quicker. I hope she was right.
Eleven. One short. I can't abide a box of twelve with a gap in it. Go and fetch the last.
Has Io still got my wick? Tell her keep it in its paper. Damp is the end of a good wick.
Thank Io for walking it out. That's the three hundredth wick I've sent to that post. I keep a tally.
Hold still. I'm trimming, and if I look up I'll cut it crooked. Talk to my hands.
Hush a moment. I'm counting how far they lean. I like to know a thing exactly before I'm frightened of it.
Lamps and wicks! Good tight wicks!
Your stool's still here, fool!
Chalk's ready, Jester! Bring me another!
Wicks! Even fools need wicks!

ribbon-dyer.guess: That wisps are colour that never took: flame that was never fixed, so it runs at the first chance, what his trade calls fugitive.
invented: His hands have been blue to the wrist since he was a boy.
He has kept the same blue vat going for forty years and feeds it every night.
He has never once got the colour of the sky after dark in a pot.
He dyed the blue cloth of the fortune-teller's tent.
He keeps a scrap of every colour he ever made in a box.
He held back one hand's length of the blue he sold the Fox.

lines.text: Evening. I bow because I'm old, and it's quicker than talking.
You've been out on the moor. It's on your boots. Peat brown. Good honest colour, that.
Late to meet. Never mind. Some colours take all night to come up.
The cold lights have no colour I could name. Not white. Not grey. Like water the dye's been washed out of.
The flames in the square have all gone a shade thinner. Yellow going to straw. A dyer sees it.
I've a word for them, for what it's worth. Fugitive. In my trade that's a colour that never took. It runs.
My steam doesn't lean now. It streams out toward the gate like a ribbon off a pole. And no wind to fly it.
I've stopped dyeing. Nothing takes tonight. Red went in the pot, came out pink, and paled on the line.
I kept back a hand's length of the Fox's blue. Habit. It's the only thing in my stall that hasn't faded tonight.
Still leaning, the flames. But they've got their colour back. Gold, not straw.
Blue holds because it sat a month in the vat. Nothing about it was quick. Except the Fox.
I can't watch the hill. I fold ribbon instead. I've folded this lot four times.
I've put a lid on the pot. First time ever. I didn't want to see which way the steam went.
Steam's going straight up. I put my hand in it to be sure. Scalded myself. Worth it.
That light on the crag. Small, warm yellow. I'll try for it in the pot tomorrow. I'll get it wrong.
You came back. People don't, to me. I say so little they think I'm cross.
I've a scrap of every colour I ever made, in a box. I'll show you one day. Not tonight.
I'll tell you. Forty years I've tried to dye the sky after dark. Never got it. You walk about in it.
You again. Stand by the pot long enough and you'll come out a different colour.
You won. There's colour up in your face. Good. Keep it.
Went under, did you. Cloth's the same. Goes in the pot dull, comes up better.
Somebody's gone pale. I know pale. I've made forty shades of it, and that's the worst.
Long enough gone for me to feed the vat twice. Welcome back.
You've been to the star tent. That blue's mine. She tells people it's the night sky. It's a week in my vat.
The pie-seller. Flour on her, always. Flour's the one white that never comes out. I've tried.
Twelve stitches of my blue, they tell me, holding twelve flames. Best work it ever did.
Held in her hands till it warmed, then off home. That's how you fix a colour, near enough. Heat and patience.
Still wet from the pot, you four. Bright. It'll shift a bit before it sets.
You four have set. Whatever comes tonight, it won't wash out of you now.
Somebody asked me what you four are like. I said deep blue, all the way through. They didn't follow.
More lamps home than out. I've put a red in the pot to see if it'll take. It's taking. Slowly.
Twelve. I sold the Fox blue enough for twelve and a bit. I don't know how she knew. I didn't ask.
Let me see that. It twitches toward the hill. And no colour in it at all. That's not thread, then.
Warm like my vat on a good morning. That's something that's been kept, not lit.
I'm stirring. If I stop, it streaks. Speak. I'll listen.
Watch the steam with me a moment. No, don't talk. Just watch where it goes.
Hot pot. Step wide.
Evening, night-blue.
Hold fast, out there.
A nod. I'm stirring.

fortune-teller.guess: That somebody has laid a fire nobody came to, and the wisps are its invitations going out.
invented: She keeps a tin for coins from true readings, and it sat empty for thirty years.
She owns only one fire card and has turned it for thirty years without believing it.
Her deck has a card numbered nothing that she thinks looks like the Jester.
The stars on her tent are painted on.
The captain has never once paid for a reading.
She keeps a cushion for people who have had bad news.
She sells charms, and hers are kept warm up her sleeve.

lines.text: Come in, come in. I'd like to tell you a pleasant lie, and tonight I can't find one anywhere.
So you're the fool who's fetching lamps. The cards told me. I'd like it noted that I didn't want them to.
At last. Every customer tonight has asked me about you four, and I've had to say I don't know. Humiliating.
Eleven shuffles, and the fire card on top every time. I only own the one.
The stars on my tent are painted on. I want that understood. Tonight I keep looking up at them anyway.
Twelve lamps gone east. I'd have warned the captain for a coin. He has never once paid for a reading.
Here's a reading, free. Somebody laid a fire and nobody came. Those lights are the invitations going out.
I've stopped charging. Being right feels too much like stealing.
I turned a card for the baker just now. A good one. I nearly kissed him. I nearly kissed the card.
All twelve home, and the deck's gone quiet. I don't trust a quiet deck. It's thinking.
The fire card came up last tonight, not first. I've done this a long time. I'm calling that progress.
I won't deal while you're up there. Not one card. If it's bad, I don't want to be the one who knew.
There's a card in my deck numbered nothing. It comes first and it comes last. It looks very like you.
I turned the fire card again just now. Same paint, same fire. It looks less lonely. Paint doesn't do that.
I've no idea what to charge for tonight. That has never happened. I may give it all back.
Back again. Second visits are half price. I've only just decided that. Tell nobody.
Your sharp-eyed one is watching my hands. Tell her the cards are honest tonight. It's me that usually isn't.
My secret. I keep a tin for coins from true readings. It sat empty for thirty years.
You're in here so often I ought to charge you rent. Sit. The chair's warm. It knows you.
You won. I could have told you that. I'm glad I didn't have to.
Flat on your back, I hear. I didn't see it coming, if that helps. I usually say I did.
One of you is hurt. Sit her down. I keep a cushion for people who've had bad news.
Where did you get to? I dealt for you while you were gone. You were fine. I checked twice.
You've talked to the singer. She'll want a last verse out of you. Don't promise one you can't pay for.
You've met the gate keeper. I read for the gate keeper once. Every card came up coins. Nobody was surprised.
Blue thread on the captain's lamps, I hear. I've no card for blue thread. I looked.
You put down the dark thing on the road? I'd have charged three coins to foretell that. I'd never have dared.
The hard cards are new to you four. No shame. Everyone's new once. I was new for years.
People come in asking how far you four will go. I've had to raise my prices.
I tried to read your fortunes just now. The cards ran out before you did.
One home. In my trade one good card means nothing. Two is a pattern. Bring me two.
All twelve. I'd have said eleven, to be safe. I'm in the business of being safe. You clearly aren't.
Cold glass. Hold it to your eye and tell me what you see. No, don't. I've had enough truth for one night.
That's not one of mine. Mine are warm because I keep them up my sleeve. That one's warm on its own.
One moment, I'm shuffling. It calms my hands. Not tonight, but usually.
Do forgive me. I was telling someone their future, and it was going badly for both of us.
Futures told! Tonight, sadly, true!
No charge for you, fool!
Don't make me right, Jester!
Palms read! Prices high!

ballad-singer.guess: That lights follow a tune out over the moor, the way they do in the old songs, and she half fears her crag song started them.
invented: She learned the crag song from her grandmother, who never knew who made it.
The crag song has a verse about an iron charm on a bracket.
She practises her bow in front of the four's wagon when they are out.
She tells each of the four, privately, that they are her favourite.

lines.text: Oh. It's you. Sorry, I go silly round you four. You're the act everyone stays for.
You're the ones out on the moor tonight. Everyone's talking. I've already started a verse. Sorry.
I've been working up the nerve to talk to you all night. Now it's late and I've forgotten every word.
I sang the crag song at dusk, and right after, the candles started leaning. I'm not singing it again.
The crowd keeps looking east between verses. Every singer knows that look. It means they're somewhere else.
In the old songs, lights always follow a tune out over the moor. I've stopped singing anything slow. Just in case.
Twelve lamps went off together, they say. Like a chorus coming in on one breath. Horrible. Beautiful. Both.
I've switched to marching songs. Loud ones. People can't be frightened and clap at the same time.
If I stop singing, the square goes so quiet you can hear the candles straining east.
Twelve home. In a song this is where they cheer and the sad part starts. Please don't let it be that sort of song.
I've started a last verse for the crag song. One line. I've crossed it out four times. It keeps ending too soon.
Nobody's watching me sing. They're all watching the hill. It's the first time I haven't minded.
You're meant to be on after me. I've sung everything I know twice. I'm keeping your spot warm.
The candles stood up straight in the middle of my chorus and I forgot every word. I didn't care.
The crag song can have a last verse now. I've not written it. I want to hear how it really went first. From you.
Again? Oh good. Don't tell the others, but you're my favourite of the four. I tell all of you that.
You laugh in the wrong places. That's where the best lines are, you know. Nobody else ever hears them.
Can I tell you something? I practise my bow in front of your wagon when you're out. Is that strange?
You'll end up in a song if you keep coming round. I'll make you rhyme with something silly.
You won? Already? I'd barely got the first verse of it written.
Knocked flat? Good. Every proper ballad has that bit. It's the bit just before the good bit.
Who's hurt? Come here. I'll sing you something soft. I promise nobody dies in it.
A lamp's come home since I saw you? That's another verse, then. This song's getting longer than the crag song.
Did she turn you a card? She told me once I'd be famous. I think she says it to every singer and means none of us.
The roaster told you his story? Count how often it changes. I've got three versions in my head already.
The captain got his pie? Good. Every song needs one person in it who gets fed and goes home happy.
One lamp home, they're shouting. I lost my place in the verse and nobody minded. That's never happened.
You four are still in the first verse. It's my favourite verse. Everything can still happen.
The ring crowd has started singing about you four. Badly. I'll fix the words later.
There'll be songs about you four when I'm an old woman. I'd like at least one of them to be mine.
Three home. Three's a good number. It's where people listening start to believe it.
All twelve. I'll put them in one by one. It'll be long. I know I said I'd keep it short.
An iron charm from the tower? The crag song has a verse about one. I always thought we'd made that up.
That's from the rush lad's fire? Somebody should write him a song. I will. He'll hate it.
Sorry, I was mid-verse. I'll finish it later. It doesn't end well anyway.
I'm resting my voice. Which means I'll talk to you for ages. It's a known problem.
Gather round! One more verse!
There's my favourite fool!
Come home safe! I've no ending yet!
Clap along, Jester!

old-lamplighter.guess: That a wisp is a flame that was blown out careless instead of capped, so it never knew it was finished and went wandering.
invented: Her mother taught her never to blow a lamp out, only to cap it.
Her round is forty-one lamps, from the fair gate out to the Last Lantern.
She saw the farm lad go up her track at noon, whistling, and has not seen him come back.
The lamp-seller once counted her wrinkles out loud.
She gives the dead post a minute after she lights it, every night, in case.

lines.text: You've come out a long way, Jester. Most folk stop at the gate. My lamps don't, so I don't.
You'll be the four, then. My round's forty-one lamps and I've not had a visitor at one of them in years.
Took you till now to come and say hello. I don't mind. Lamps and old women, we're used to waiting.
My lamp's leaning east and there's not a breath of wind. I've put my hand round it. It doesn't help. It's company.
Lit the dead post at dusk like always. Tonight I watched the flame leave. It didn't go out. It went.
Those lights out in the heather want fetching. They're none of mine, but I'd not leave a dog out on a night like this.
My mother said never blow a lamp out. Cap it. A blown flame doesn't know it's done. It wanders.
I'm not going back to the fair. Somebody has to stand here so the lights going home know where the road is.
I watched your herb-witch hold one like a hurt bird till it went warm. All my years of lamps, I never thought to try.
Heather's dark again. No lights in it but mine. That's how a moor ought to look at night.
My lamp still leans, mind. I've tied my hanky round the post. Don't laugh. It's like holding its hand.
I can see the ship up by the crag. Twelve lamps in a row, like a round. Somebody keep them lit.
My lamp's tugging on its hook like a child that wants to go and look. I've told it no. It's sulking.
Both posts are lit. The dead one too. A light came down off the hill and sat in it like it had never been gone.
That post's held since the light came down. I'm not crying, it's the smoke. There isn't any smoke.
Come out twice, have you? Bring that cold over by the lamp. It'll see to you.
My lamp likes you, I think. It burns a bit taller when you're stood there. Don't let it go to your head.
You want to know why I light that dead post every night? Somebody has to. A lamp should know it's expected.
Out here again. I've started leaving you the lee side of the post. The lamp's not pleased. That's its side.
You won, by the look of you. Good. Now do your shouting further up the track. My lamp's nervous.
One of you's limping. Lean on my post a minute, love. It's held me up for years.
Thought you'd gone. I kept the lamp up bright in case you needed finding.
Another lamp got home, has it? Good. I don't like any lamp out on the moor with nobody to light it.
You've seen the lamp-seller. Is she still counting everything? She counted my wrinkles once. Out loud.
You found the rush lad by the pool? Is he warm? He went up my track at noon, whistling. I've not heard him since.
Ship's lamps, the lights in my heather? No wonder they've no posts. Poor things, a long way off their hooks.
That dark thing by the stones is gone? I felt it up there all evening. It never turned to my lamp. Only up the hill.
You four jump at every shadow on the track. Good. I did, my first year. It means you're looking.
You walk this track like you've a round of your own now. Straight down the middle. No looking back.
The heather goes quiet when you four come down the track. I've only ever heard it do that for weather.
Some home already? Good. I never sleep while there's a lamp out on this moor. Not that I sleep at night anyway.
All twelve. Not one of them stopped by my post to say goodnight. Ship's lamps. No manners.
Is that her wick your herb-witch is carrying? Bring it here, then. We'll watch it not work together.
Tell her the wick was good. I'll want another tomorrow. Don't tell her I said it was good.
Hush a minute, I'm lighting. A flame likes quiet while it's catching.
I'm watching the dead post. I always give it a minute after. In case. Stand with me.
Mind the ruts, there!
Evening, love! Lamp's still lit!
Go on. I'll keep the road lit!
Don't fight near my lamp!

farm-lad.guess: That wisps are lights nobody was watching: look away for one minute and off they go, which is why he will not take his eyes off his fire.
invented: He has cut rushes for the fair's ponies since he was small, and they expect him home.
His lantern was his grandad's, and his grandad is still alive to hear about tonight.
It took him nine strikes of his flint to light the fire.
He went up the track at noon, whistling, past the lamplighter.

lines.text: Oh, it's you lot. It is, isn't it? From the fair? Sorry, I can't look up. I'm minding the fire.
The Jester. At my fire. Wait till the ponies hear. They won't care. I'll tell them anyway.
You've come all the way out here? To me? Nobody at the fair's going to believe it. I don't believe it. Sit down.
My lantern went off up the hill like a pony that's heard the feed bucket. I never called it. Honest.
Took nine goes with the flint to light this. Nine. It's not going anywhere now. I won't let it.
If you ask me, they're lights nobody was watching. I looked away from my lantern for one minute. One.
A string of lights came down over the far bank, like starlings settling. They've not moved since. I'm not going over.
I've had this fire going since the sun went. Is it still the same night? It feels like about four nights.
Saw a little light go back past me toward the fair, all warm and gold. I nearly waved at it. I did wave.
The far bank's gone dark. No more lights in the reeds. Does that mean you've got them all? It does, doesn't it.
It's gone quieter. I heard a bird just now, first one all night. I nearly cried. I didn't. Nearly, though.
I saw a ship go over toward the crag with all its lamps lit. Was that you? It was, wasn't it. I knew it.
My fire's leaning up the hill harder than all night. I've got my boot against the stones. Feels like helping.
I looked away just now. On purpose. Counted to ten. When I looked back it was still there. It just stayed.
There's a little light in the heather by my boot. I think it's my lantern's, come home. It's the right yellow.
You're back. I saved you the dry end of the log.
I've told the fire all about you. It went up a bit when I said the Jester. I'm not making that up.
Can I ask you something? Do you get frightened when you fight? You never look it. How do you not look it?
You come out here more than I go home. Have you got a fire of your own you're avoiding?
Was that you? Did you win? You won. You've got the look the ponies get after a good gallop.
You got knocked down? You? I didn't know you could fall over. I thought you sort of floated.
Sit down by the fire, all of you. It's a good fire. It's warm and it doesn't wander off.
You were gone that long I ran out of sticks and started on the rushes. The ponies will be furious.
The lamplighter's all right? Her lamp's still lit? I kept thinking of her down there on her own. She'd say she's fine.
You've been talking to the baker? Don't tell me what was in his oven. I'll only cry.
It's gone off the road? Really gone? Then I could walk home. I'm not going to. But I could.
Your herb-witch warmed one and it went home? So they're not bad, they're lost. Like my lantern. Oh.
You four look a bit how I feel. No offence. I mean it nicely. Like you're still finding out.
You walk like you know where your feet go. I tried walking like that. I fell in the rushes.
My grandad will want to hear about you. Every bit. I'll be telling it till I'm his age.
That's most of them back? Can I help carry? I'm good at carrying. I'd have to bring the fire.
All twelve? I want to shout. Can I shout? I'm going to shout. Quietly. The pool's listening.
That's my stone. Out of my fire ring. Is it still warm? It is. I'm going to be proud of that for years.
That thread keeps twitching up the hill. Put it away, please. I don't want my fire getting ideas.
Come and warm up. There's room on the log. Only don't stand in front of the fire. I have to see it.
One stick at a time. Too many and it roars, and roaring's how they start leaving. There. What is it?
Hello! You're from the fair!
Jester! I kept it going!
Careful on that road, Jester!
Still watching it!
Your steam's leaning the same way as my flames. I measured. Same angle, near enough.
Near enough.
You might say more than two words tonight, of all nights.
I might. Then I'd have said them.
I turned the fire card for the Jester. The one with nobody by it. She paid, and laughed.
A fire with nobody by it. I've thirty-one of those on my counter. We call them lamps.
It isn't funny.
No. Sit down. You're too tall to be frightened standing up.
Read me something nice. Anything. Make it up if you have to.
I don't make things up, darling. I arrange them attractively.
Then arrange me something with a happy ending.
On a night like this? That's extra.
Have you any blue left? I wanted a bit for my hem before the four go on.
The Fox has it.
All of it? What on earth does she want with all of it?
Sewing.
If I sing the crag song now, will your flames lean worse?
Sing it and I'll count them.
And if they do lean worse?
Then sing something about sheep.
You dyed my tent. Be honest with me. Are the stars too much?
Last year they were.
And tonight?
Tonight I'd paint on more.
She lit my wick on the dead post. It leaned and went out. She says it's never the wick.
It isn't.
You've never even seen that post.
I've seen your wicks.
Did you hear? The Fox sewed every flame down with your blue. Twelve stitches.
I heard.
Aren't you proud? You should be shouting it from the awning.
I am.
Deal one card for them. Just one. I won't hold you to it.
I dealt one when the ship went up. I put it back face down.
You didn't look?
Darling, I've been right all night. I'd like to be surprised once.
I've given three coins back tonight. Three. I don't know what's come over me.
It's going round. I've given away two lamps and a box of wicks.
You counted them, I suppose.
Forty-four wicks. I'll not ask for them back. I'll think about it.
Lamps keep going out behind me. Every row. I've relit your wicks three times tonight.
It's not my wicks.
I know it's not. Forty years, and I've never had one of yours quit.
Then it's something new. I've never cared for new.
Pie, love. You've had nothing since dusk. Don't tell me you have, I've been watching.
I'm stirring.
Stir with one hand, eat with the other. It's mutton, before you ask.
I wasn't going to.
The captain's lamps came off their hooks and went over my bar. All twelve. East.
I know. I've had a card saying something of the sort since dusk.
Next time, tell the gate.
My coals went grey as those lamps went over, then came back. Put that in a song.
What rhymes with coals?
Holes. Bowls. Moles.
I'm not singing about moles. Not tonight. Maybe tomorrow.
